title: Team of Teams
author: Stanley McChrystal
theme: In a fast, interconnected world, organisations win through adaptability, built by linking small teams through shared awareness and trusted, decentralised decision-making.
summary: General Stanley McChrystal, writing with several colleagues, draws on his time leading a US special operations task force in Iraq. His forces were better trained, better equipped and better funded than the insurgent network they fought, yet they kept losing ground. The enemy was loose, fast and able to change shape. The task force was a superb machine built for a slower, more predictable world.

The book traces that mismatch to the management thinking of the industrial age. Breaking work into specialised parts and controlling it from the top made organisations highly efficient. Efficiency works well when problems are merely complicated and can be planned in advance. It fails when problems are complex: when countless interacting factors make the future impossible to predict. In such conditions, the ability to adapt matters more than the ability to optimise.

Small teams already adapt well. Their members trust one another, share a purpose and understand the whole situation, so they can react to surprises without waiting for orders. The trouble is that a large organisation made of excellent teams can still behave badly, because the teams compete, hoard information and see only their own piece of the problem.

The answer McChrystal describes is a team of teams: giving the whole organisation the qualities of a single good team. Two practices made this possible. The first was shared consciousness. The task force opened up information radically, held a daily briefing that thousands of people joined, and placed its people inside partner agencies to build relationships and understanding. The second was empowered execution. Once people understood the big picture, decisions could be pushed down to those closest to the action, which made the organisation far faster.

This changes the leader's role. Instead of directing every move like a chess player, the leader acts more like a gardener, shaping the environment, setting culture and keeping the system healthy so others can act well.
takeaway: Share information widely so everyone sees the whole picture, then trust people close to the action to decide, and lead by tending the system rather than controlling every move.

questions.q: What problem did McChrystal's task force face at the start of the story?
options: It lacked funding and modern equipment
It was efficient but too slow and rigid to keep up with a fast, decentralised enemy network
Its soldiers were poorly trained
It had no clear chain of command
questions.why: The task force had every material advantage but was structured for predictability, not speed and adaptation.

questions.q: According to the book, what is the key difference between a complicated problem and a complex one?
options: Complicated problems are always larger
Complex problems involve only technology
Complex problems have so many interacting factors that outcomes cannot be reliably predicted
Complicated problems cannot be solved at all
questions.why: Complicated systems can be analysed and planned; complex ones behave unpredictably because of their many interactions.

questions.q: Which quality does the book argue matters most in a complex environment?
options: Adaptability
Efficiency
Standardisation
Strict hierarchy
questions.why: The book contends that efficiency built for predictable conditions must give way to the ability to adapt.

questions.q: Where does the book locate the roots of the efficiency-focused management model?
options: Ancient military empires
The digital start-up culture
Medieval craft guilds
Industrial-age scientific management and specialisation
questions.why: It links the model to industrial thinking that broke work into specialised parts controlled from the top.

questions.q: Why can an organisation built from excellent small teams still perform poorly?
options: Small teams are always too slow
The teams may compete, hoard information and see only their own part of the problem
Small teams cannot be trained effectively
Teams need more managers to function
questions.why: Strong teams can form silos, so the whole fails to act as one.

questions.q: What does 'shared consciousness' mean in the book?
options: Everyone follows the same written procedures
Leaders keep sensitive information to a small inner circle
Broad, transparent information sharing so people across the organisation understand the whole situation
All decisions are made by group vote
questions.why: Shared consciousness is about giving everyone a common, system-wide view through openness.

questions.q: Which practice did the task force use to build shared consciousness?
options: A daily briefing open to a very large number of participants
Reducing meetings to once a month
Restricting information on a strict need-to-know basis
Replacing teams with individual specialists
questions.why: The large daily briefing let people across units and agencies see the same picture.

options: Leaders personally approving every action
Handing all decisions to outside consultants
Removing all goals so people can do as they like
Pushing decisions down to the people closest to the action once they understand the big picture
questions.why: With shared context, front-line people could decide quickly without waiting for approval from above.

questions.q: Why did the task force place its people inside partner agencies?
options: To monitor them for mistakes
To build trust and relationships across organisational boundaries
To take over those agencies' work
To reduce its own headcount
questions.why: Embedding people helped break down silos and build connections between organisations.

questions.q: Which metaphor does McChrystal use for the leader's new role?
options: A conductor controlling every note
A referee enforcing rules
A gardener who tends the environment so others can grow and act
A general who plans each step in advance
questions.why: The gardener shapes conditions and culture rather than directing every move like a chess player.
